title: Tokens, sessions & logout
summary: How an authenticated session is kept alive, validated, and torn down: refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, introspection vs. local JWT validation and revocation, the three OIDC logout mechanisms, and how to choose a session representation without reaching for deprecated flows.

lessons.title: Refresh tokens & rotation with reuse detection
lessons.objective: Renew access without re-prompting the user, and detect a stolen refresh token.
lessons.content:
Access tokens are deliberately short-lived, but users stay signed in far longer. A refresh token bridges the gap: the client presents it at the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token and receives a fresh access token — no user interaction. For OIDC the client asks for this capability with the offline_access scope, subject to consent.

Rotation hardens this. On each refresh the authorization server issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. Public clients (SPAs, native apps) must rotate; confidential clients should, or sender-constrain instead.

Rotation is what makes reuse detection possible. Once a refresh token has been rotated away, it should never be seen again. If an already-used token is presented, two parties hold copies — one of them is a thief. The AS cannot tell which, so it revokes the entire token family and forces interactive re-authentication. Every reuse trip is a probable theft: log and alert on it.

Two expiry models bound the family: sliding expiry extends an idle window on each refresh, while absolute expiry sets a hard ceiling from initial authorization. Robust deployments combine them — a sliding idle timeout capped by an absolute lifetime. On refresh you may narrow scope with the scope parameter, never widen it. Errors surface as invalid_grant (expired, revoked, reused, or unknown token).

lessons.title: Validating tokens: introspection vs. local JWT validation, and revocation
lessons.objective: Decide how a resource server checks a token, and understand what revocation actually does.
lessons.content:
A resource server holding a bearer token has two ways to trust it, and they trade freshness against scale.

Local JWT validation — a self-contained JWT is verified against the issuer's signing keys (JWKS) with no network call. Fast and stateless, but the token stays valid until its exp: you cannot un-issue it early.

Introspection (RFC 7662) — for opaque reference tokens the API POSTs the token to /introspect with its own client credentials and reads back active (true/false) plus metadata like scope, aud, exp, and a cnf claim for sender-constrained tokens. Introspection reflects revocation immediately, at the cost of a round trip — cache positive results only up to exp. The endpoint MUST authenticate its caller and return exactly {"active":false} for an inactive token, or it becomes a token oracle.

Revocation (RFC 7009) is the write side of the same lifecycle. A client POSTs to /revoke; the AS returns 200 even for an unknown token, deliberately, so the endpoint can't be used to probe validity. Revoking a refresh token cascades to its access tokens (and, under rotation, the whole family). Whether an API sees the effect at once depends on how it validates: introspection catches it immediately, a local JWT survives until exp. That is why revocation is paired with short access-token lifetimes.

lessons.title: Logout done right: RP-initiated, front-channel, back-channel
lessons.objective: Distinguish the three OIDC logout mechanisms and see why single logout is hard.
lessons.content:
Signing out of one app is easy; signing out of an SSO session shared by many apps is not. OIDC splits the problem into three specifications.

RP-Initiated Logout starts it. The Relying Party clears its own session, then redirects the browser to the IdP's end_session_endpoint with an id_token_hint and a pre-registered post_logout_redirect_uri. The IdP ends its own SSO session and redirects back. This ends the session at the IdP — but not at the other RPs that joined the same SSO session.

Propagating to those other RPs is a separate concern with two mechanisms. Front-Channel Logout runs through the browser: the IdP's logout page renders one hidden iframe per RP, each loading that RP's frontchannel_logout_uri to clear its cookie. It needs no server-to-server path, but it is best-effort — modern browsers partition or block third-party cookies (Safari ITP, Firefox ETP, Chrome), the IdP gets no confirmation, and CSP or X-Frame-Options can silently kill a frame, so expect partial logout. Back-Channel Logout is the reliable path: the IdP POSTs a signed logout token (a JWT with an events claim plus sub and/or sid) directly to each RP's backchannel_logout_uri, no browser involved. The RP validates it like an ID token — signature, iss, aud, events, and no nonce — then destroys the matching sessions.

Single logout is hard because every RP must cooperate, front-channel delivery is unverifiable, and clearing a session does not revoke tokens already issued: access tokens live until exp unless the RP also revokes or introspects. Keep them short-lived as a backstop.

lessons.title: Choosing sessions vs. tokens (and avoiding the deprecated Implicit flow)
lessons.objective: Pick a session representation on purpose, and recognize why Implicit was replaced.
lessons.content:
How should a system remember an authenticated user across requests? Three shapes, with the same underlying tension — revocation and freshness versus scale and statelessness, plus the browser-security profile (XSS vs. CSRF).

Server-side session cookie — an opaque ID in an HttpOnly cookie, with state in a session store. Revocation is instant (delete the session); ideal for classic first-party web apps.

Stateless JWT — a self-contained signed token verified locally, scaling without any central lookup. The cost is revocation: it needs short TTLs plus a denylist to un-issue early.

Reference token + introspection — an opaque bearer token the API introspects (or caches) at the AS, giving central revocation while keeping the token contents opaque.

Whatever you choose, do not reach for the ⛔ deprecated Implicit flow. It returned tokens directly in the redirect URL fragment, exposing them to browser history, referrer leakage, and script access, with no client authentication and no refresh-token rotation. The OAuth 2.0 Security BCP forbids response_type=token and OAuth 2.1 removes the flow entirely. Its replacement is Authorization Code + PKCE: a code exchanged over the back channel, proof-bound with PKCE, and eligible for refresh-token rotation. Migrating a legacy SPA means switching response_type from id_token token to code plus PKCE, and rotating any long-lived tokens issued under Implicit.

quiz.q: A previously rotated refresh token is presented again at the token endpoint. What should the authorization server do?
choices: Silently issue a new access token; rotation makes replay harmless
Revoke the entire token family and force interactive re-authentication
Return the same access token it issued the first time
Extend the family's sliding expiry window
quiz.explain: A rotated token should never be seen again. Its reuse means two parties hold copies and one is a thief. The AS cannot tell which, so it revokes the whole family and forces re-authentication — this is reuse detection.

quiz.q: A resource server validates a self-contained JWT locally against the JWKS. An admin revokes that token. When does the API stop honoring it?
choices: Immediately, because revocation propagates to JWKS
Not until the token's exp, unless the API also introspects or checks a denylist
After the next refresh rotation
Only when the user next signs in
quiz.explain: Local JWT validation is stateless: the token stays valid until exp regardless of revocation. To get immediate effect, validate via introspection (which reflects revocation at once) or keep access-token lifetimes short.

quiz.q: Why does the RFC 7009 revocation endpoint return 200 even for a token it has never seen?
choices: To signal the token was successfully created
So the endpoint cannot be used as an oracle to probe token validity
Because unknown tokens are always still active
To trigger a retry from the client
quiz.explain: Returning 200 for unknown or already-invalid tokens is deliberate: a differentiated response would let a caller test whether a given token is valid. The endpoint must not become a validity oracle.

quiz.q: Which logout mechanism is the reliable one for propagating a single logout to other RPs, and why?
choices: Front-channel, because iframes always render
RP-initiated, because it clears the IdP session
Back-channel, because the IdP POSTs a signed logout token server-to-server with no dependence on browser cookies
They are equally reliable
quiz.explain: Front-channel logout runs through browser iframes and is best-effort — third-party-cookie blocking and CSP cause partial logout, with no confirmation to the IdP. Back-channel logout delivers a validated logout-token JWT directly to each RP, independent of the browser, so it is the reliable path.

quiz.q: A legacy SPA uses the OIDC Implicit flow (response_type=id_token token). What is the recommended migration?
choices: Keep Implicit but add longer token lifetimes
Switch to the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant
Move to Authorization Code + PKCE and rotate any long-lived tokens issued under Implicit
Add a silent-renewal iframe to keep it compliant
quiz.explain: Implicit is deprecated: it leaks tokens in the URL fragment, has no client authentication, and cannot use refresh-token rotation. The Security BCP and OAuth 2.1 replace it with Authorization Code + PKCE — a back-channel code exchange bound with PKCE.
